predictions: At fixed mass ratio, pericenter, gas fraction and pre-encounter structure, normalized integrated EnergyDissipation plus radiative cooling predicts a larger decrease in visible relative orbital energy and a shorter coalescence time.

At matched instantaneous separation, relative speed, mass ratio and gas fraction, post-pericenter systems have a larger residual loss rate than first-infall systems only for a memory bath; an instantaneous shock law has no history residual after its measured gas state is controlled.

The bimodal bath predicts a fast approximately one-Gyr decay and a distinct slow persistence tail in phase-space distance; the frozen constants are calibrated only to the published one-object Illustris benchmark and must be tested without retuning on TNG100-1.
Any visible orbital angular-momentum deficit must be balanced by gas/internal spin, outflow or radiative flux within the declared aperture ledger.

A matched TNG100-1-Dark history can show collisionless mixing and clumping without positive gas receiver flux; morphology or phase-space persistence alone is therefore insufficient evidence for dissipation.

The candidate must outperform Newtonian time-dependent collisionless evolution, standard shock/cooling, the Boylan-Kolchin extended-satellite merger-time law, dissipative-DM cooling/gravothermal-collapse models, and flexible history controls before a new-gravity interpretation is considered.
